title: HTTP Methods and Status Codes
description: Master the five core HTTP methods used in REST APIs and learn which HTTP status codes to return in every scenario. Understand idempotency, safety, and how to communicate success, client errors, and server failures clearly.

blocks.text: HTTP methods and status codes are the communication protocol between client and server. The method tells the server what the client wants to do, and the status code tells the client what happened. Using the right combination makes your API predictable and easy to debug.
The Core HTTP Methods

There are several HTTP methods, but five are used in virtually every REST API: GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, and DELETE. Each method has a well-defined meaning. Using them consistently is one of the hallmarks of a well-designed API.
GET — Retrieve a Resource

GET is used to fetch a resource or collection of resources. It is the safest HTTP method — it should never modify server state. GET requests can be cached by browsers and intermediaries, and they can be bookmarked or shared. A GET request to /api/products should always return the same result (assuming no one else changed the data in the meantime).
POST — Create a Resource

POST is used to create a new resource. Unlike GET, POST is not idempotent — calling it twice creates two separate resources. POST requests are never cached. The server decides the new resource's identifier and returns it in the response, typically with a 201 Created status and a Location header.
PUT — Replace a Resource

PUT replaces an entire resource with the provided representation. It is idempotent — calling PUT three times with the same data produces the same result as calling it once. PUT requires the client to send the complete resource, not just the fields that changed.
PATCH — Partially Update a Resource

PATCH applies partial modifications to a resource. Use it when the client only needs to update specific fields rather than replacing the entire resource. For example, updating just the price of a product is a PATCH operation, not a PUT.
DELETE — Remove a Resource

DELETE removes a resource identified by the URI. It is idempotent — deleting a resource that does not exist still returns a successful status (often 204 or 404 depending on your design choice). Once a DELETE succeeds, subsequent GET requests to that URI should return 404.

blocks.text: HTTP Status Codes

Status codes are three-digit numbers sent by the server in the response. The first digit indicates the category: 1xx for informational, 2xx for success, 3xx for redirects, 4xx for client errors, and 5xx for server errors. For REST APIs, you will primarily use 2xx, 4xx, and 5xx codes.

blocks.title: Return Accurate Status Codes
blocks.text: Returning 200 OK for a failed operation is one of the most common API design mistakes. A client that always receives 200 cannot distinguish between success and failure without inspecting the response body. Use the right code so clients can handle errors automatically.
2xx Success Codes

200 OK is the most common success code, used for GET requests that retrieve data and PUT/PATCH requests that update data. 201 Created signals that a new resource was created — it is the standard response for POST. 204 No Content is used for DELETE requests and some PUT requests where there is no data to return.
4xx Client Error Codes

400 Bad Request means the client sent malformed data or the request failed validation. 401 Unauthorized means the client is not authenticated. 403 Forbidden means the client is authenticated but does not have permission. 404 Not Found means the requested resource does not exist. 409 Conflict means the request could not be completed due to a conflict with the current state of the resource.
5xx Server Error Codes

500 Internal Server Error is the generic catch-all for unexpected server failures. 503 Service Unavailable means the server is temporarily unable to handle the request, often due to maintenance or overload. Try to avoid 500s by catching expected exceptions and returning more specific error codes where possible.

blocks.text: Idempotency and Safety

An idempotent method produces the same server state no matter how many times it is called with the same input. GET, PUT, and DELETE are idempotent. POST is not — two POST requests create two separate resources. A safe method is one that does not modify server state. Only GET is truly safe.

Understanding idempotency matters for network reliability. If a client sends a PUT request and loses its network connection before receiving a response, it can safely retry the request. The server state will be the same whether the first request arrived or not. The same cannot be said for POST.

blocks.title: Key Terms: HTTP Methods and Status Codes

terms.definition: HTTP method to retrieve a resource. Safe, idempotent, and cacheable. Never modifies server state.
HTTP method to create a new resource. Not idempotent — each call creates a separate resource.
An operation whose result is the same whether called once or many times. PUT and DELETE are idempotent.
Status code returned after a successful POST that created a new resource. Includes a Location header.
Status code returned when the requested resource does not exist on the server.

blocks.title: Common Status Code Pairs
blocks.text: 200 OK pairs with GET and PUT. 201 Created pairs with POST. 204 No Content pairs with DELETE. 404 Not Found pairs with GET, PUT, PATCH, and DELETE when the resource is missing. 400 Bad Request pairs with POST, PUT, and PATCH when the input is invalid.

blocks.title: Lesson Summary: HTTP Methods and Status Codes
points: GET retrieves resources safely and is the only idempotent, cacheable method
POST creates new resources and is not idempotent — each call creates a separate item
PUT replaces an entire resource and is idempotent — the same call always produces the same result
PATCH partially updates specific fields — use it when the client only changes a subset of fields
DELETE removes resources and is idempotent — deleting an already-deleted item is still a success
200 OK, 201 Created, and 204 No Content are the primary success codes for API responses
blocks.takeaway: HTTP methods and status codes give your API a contract. Clients know what to expect from each operation and can handle responses programmatically. Consistency in these conventions is what separates professional APIs from ad-hoc ones.

blocks.title: Exercise: Map HTTP Methods and Status Codes to API Actions
blocks.description: Given a resource type, write the full set of controller actions with the correct HTTP method attributes, return types, and status codes.
steps: Choose a resource type (e.g., Reviews, Invoices, InventoryItems)
Write a GET action that returns all items with a 200 OK response
Write a GET action that returns a single item by ID, returning 404 if not found
Write a POST action that creates a new item and returns 201 Created with a Location header
Write a PUT action that replaces an item entirely and returns 204 No Content on success
Write a PATCH action that updates a single field and returns 200 OK with the updated item
blocks.expectedOutcome: A complete set of five action methods, each decorated with the correct HTTP method attribute and returning the appropriate status code for every possible outcome (success, not found, validation error).

blocks.title: HTTP Methods and Status Codes Checklist

items.text: I can explain the difference between idempotent and non-idempotent methods
items.hint: Idempotent means the same call produces the same result every time. GET, PUT, DELETE are idempotent. POST is not.

items.text: I know which status code to return after a successful POST
items.hint: 201 Created with a Location header pointing to the new resource.

items.text: I know which status code to return after a successful DELETE
items.hint: 204 No Content — there is nothing to return after deletion.

items.text: I understand when to return 400 vs 404 vs 500
items.hint: 400 = bad request data, 404 = resource not found, 500 = unexpected server failure.

items.text: I can explain why PUT is idempotent but POST is not
items.hint: PUT replaces the resource at a known URI — same input, same result. POST creates a new item each time.
